title: How Coral Reefs Recover
context: A university lecture on what a damaged coral reef needs in order to recover.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text:
Good afternoon. Last week we looked at what damages a coral reef. Today I want to look at the other half of the question, which is much less often asked: what does a reef actually need in order to come back?

Let me start with the event itself. When water stays warmer than a coral can tolerate for a sustained period, the coral expels the algae that live inside its tissue and give it both its colour and most of its food. That is bleaching. It is important to understand that a bleached coral is not a dead coral. It is a starving one. If temperatures fall within a few weeks, the algae can be taken back up and the animal survives, though it will usually not reproduce that year. If the heat persists, the coral dies, and what is left is a skeleton.

Recovery from that point depends on three things, and they are not equally likely to be present.

The first is larvae. Corals reproduce by releasing eggs and sperm into the water, often in a single synchronised mass spawning, and the larvae that result drift before settling. A damaged reef can be restocked by larvae from its own surviving colonies or from a healthy reef upstream in the prevailing current. This is why the position of a reef within a network matters more than its own condition. An isolated reef that loses its corals has no source of new larvae and may not recover in any human timescale, while a reef of identical damage sitting downstream of a healthy one can be repopulated within a decade.

The second is a surface the larvae can attach to. A coral larva will not settle on loose rubble that shifts with every storm, and a dead reef often becomes exactly that. It settles preferentially on hard, stable substrate coated with a particular family of pink encrusting algae, which appear to release a chemical cue the larvae detect. Where storm damage has reduced a reef structure to mobile fragments, the biological problem is not the absence of larvae at all. They arrive, and they have nowhere to hold on.

The third is grazing, and it is the one most often overlooked. When corals die, fast-growing seaweed colonises the space within months. If nothing eats that seaweed, it holds the space indefinitely and coral larvae cannot compete. What eats it is a specific set of herbivorous fish — parrotfish above all — and sea urchins. A reef whose herbivores have been fished out can be given perfect water temperature and abundant larvae and still fail to recover, because the space is already occupied. This is the clearest case in reef ecology of a system that has two stable states: coral-dominated and seaweed-dominated, with the difference maintained by who is eating.

There is evidence for this from an accident rather than an experiment. In the Caribbean in the early 1980s a disease killed the great majority of one urchin species across the whole region within about a year. Reefs that had already lost most of their large herbivorous fish to fishing shifted to seaweed and, in many places, have not shifted back in forty years. Reefs where fish populations were intact fared considerably better with the same urchin losses.

That points to the practical conclusion, which is uncomfortable for anyone hoping for a technical fix. Coral gardening — growing fragments in nurseries and transplanting them — works at the scale of hectares and costs a great deal per hectare. The world's reefs cover something over a quarter of a million square kilometres. Transplanting cannot be the answer at that scale, and the projects that have succeeded are almost all ones where the underlying conditions were already suitable and the intervention simply accelerated a recovery that would have happened anyway.

What does scale is protecting the herbivores and the connectivity. A network of reserves placed so that healthy reefs sit upstream of damaged ones, with fishing controls that keep parrotfish populations intact, costs a fraction of transplanting and works on the mechanism rather than the symptom. It is less satisfying to photograph, which I suspect is part of why it is harder to fund.

Next week we will look at the thermal tolerance question — whether corals can adapt fast enough — and I will ask you to have read the Hughes review before then.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.sentence: During bleaching a coral expels the ___ that live in its tissue.
questions.explanation: “The coral expels the algae that live inside its tissue and give it both its colour and most of its food.”

questions.sentence: The lecturer says a bleached coral is not dead but ___.
questions.explanation: “It is important to understand that a bleached coral is not a dead coral. It is a starving one.”

questions.sentence: Larvae will not settle on loose ___ that moves in storms.
questions.explanation: “A coral larva will not settle on loose rubble that shifts with every storm.”

questions.sentence: Larvae prefer hard substrate coated with pink encrusting ___.
questions.explanation: “It settles preferentially on hard, stable substrate coated with a particular family of pink encrusting algae, which appear to release a chemical cue.”

questions.sentence: Among herbivorous fish, ___ are named as the most important grazers.
questions.explanation: “A specific set of herbivorous fish — parrotfish above all — and sea urchins.”

questions.sentence: Reef ecology describes coral and seaweed dominance as two stable ___.
questions.explanation: “A system that has two stable states: coral-dominated and seaweed-dominated, with the difference maintained by who is eating.”

questions.question: According to the lecturer, which THREE factors does a dead reef's recovery depend on?
options: Enough coral larvae reaching the reef
A stable surface for larvae to attach to
Sufficient grazing by herbivorous fish and sea urchins
Sea temperature returning to its normal range
The genetic diversity of the surviving coral
questions.explanation: The lecturer lists the three directly: “The first is larvae”, “The second is a surface the larvae can attach to”, and “The third is grazing” — supporting the first, second and third options. Temperature is discussed earlier, but only as the trigger that reverses bleaching in a coral that is still alive; it is not one of the three things a dead reef needs in order to recover, so the fourth option does not belong on this list. Coral gardening is described as unable to work “at the scale of the world's reefs”, which rules out the fifth option, and neither funding nor genetic diversity is mentioned anywhere in the lecture, so the sixth and seventh options are both unsupported.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: What is the lecturer's view of coral gardening?
options: It is the most promising large-scale solution
It cannot work at the scale of the world's reefs
It should be stopped because it damages nurseries
questions.explanation: It works “at the scale of hectares” against reefs covering “over a quarter of a million square kilometres”, so “transplanting cannot be the answer at that scale”.
